home-energy-audit.h1: Home energy audits in Saint John
home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Saint John: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Saint John: 4 licensed organizations, local prices, New Brunswick rebates and what 78% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 4 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Saint John. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Saint John houses, and which New Brunswick rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Saint John homes
sections.html:
Of Saint John's 19,705 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 78% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Saint John house dates from 1961–1970, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Saint John gets about 4,580 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.5°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Saint John. That's about 16% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Saint John area, 38% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards and 32% with a heat pump; electricity is the main heating energy for 46% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

sections.h2: What it costs in Saint John
sections.html: Through the Total Home Energy Savings Program, a Certified Energy Advisor charges $99 + HST, covering both the initial and final evaluations.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.h1: Heat loss calculations in Saint John
heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Saint John: sizing a heat pump for −22.5°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Saint John homes, sized to the local −22.5°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −22.5°C for Saint John, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Saint John.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Saint John
sections.html:
−22.5°C is the 27th-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −22.5°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Saint John area, 38% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards and 32% with a heat pump; electricity is the main heating energy for 46% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

glance.sub: the Saint John, NB (Saint John CMA) metro area

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Saint John homes
sections.html:
Saint John gets about 4,580 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.5°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Saint John. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mold usually starts in Saint John houses.

Of Saint John's 19,705 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 78% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Ask any Saint John tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Saint John · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.
